Article Title: Scientists in Thailand hid fruits in an opaque box; 16 Asian elephants learned to navigate it for rewards and followed it along
Article Text:
A fruit reward

Older elephants took longer time

The transparent box needs a careful reading

What this could mean for conservation

Asian elephants can abandon a familiar way of reaching food when it stops working, as per a new study conducted in Thailand. In tests with 16 animals, researchers found evidence of inhibitory control, the ability to hold back an unhelpful response and switch to a successful one in seconds.The research, published in PLOS One on September 9, 2026, offered a closer look at how elephants adjust to changing circumstances. The most revealing moment arrived when scientists moved the route to a fruit, forcing the animals to overcome their habit, one they had just learned.Sydney Hope of Hunter College and colleagues tested Asian elephants at Thailand's National Elephant Institute. They set up a box with a practical problem for an animal with a long, flexible trunk, with the box having a fruit in front of them, but a barrier blocking the direct approach.First, the elephants learned to reach around an opaque box and put their trunks through its opening to retrieve the fruit reward. Then, researchers substituted a transparent box with small holes in the front, allowing the animals to see and smell the reward but with an opening elsewhere.The elephants continued reaching around the barrier, showing that they could successfully shift to the indirect approach even with the food visible in front of them, and not be distracted by the sight of it.Next, the team rotated the box so that the opening was in a different position. Initially, the elephants returned to the place that had previously provided access, even though reaching there did not work. Then, they adjusted and found the new entrance.The study's measurements captured the disruption. After a rotation in the opening, the average time from first touching to getting their trunk in the opening rose from about 2.2 seconds to 8.2 seconds. Also, performance improved over repeated attempts due to the opening being in the same position.Age added another layer to the experiment and the findings. Older elephants were slower to adapt when the opening was rotated, suggesting that suppressing a previously successful response may become difficult later in life. The participants ranged from 4 to 60 years old, but the small sample leaned toward younger animals. A wider spread of ages would help researchers determine how consistently the pattern appears. For now, the authors treat cognitive decline as a possible explanation requiring further study. The distinction matters because a slower response in one task says little about an animal’s full range of abilities. Researchers still need to establish how performance in this particular situation relates to the other demands elephants faceThe authors caution that seeing and smelling the fruit may never have triggered a strong impulse to reach straight ahead, so the animals could simply have continued a practised movement. The rotation trials supplied the clearer evidence because they exposed an initial mistake followed by adjustment. That sequence supports the researchers’ interpretation of inhibitory control, while leaving open questions about how broadly the ability operates in everyday elephant life.“This ability may be important for elephants’ social interactions or for other aspects of cognition, such as problem-solving,” Hope said in a CUNY statement. Those possible connections give researchers something to investigate next, including whether this kind of behavioural flexibility helps elephants coordinate with companions or tackle unfamiliar challenges.The experiment extends beyond just a test. Asian elephants encounter farms and settlements across landscapes shared with people, and crop damage can put both communities and animals at risk. Understanding how elephants respond to obstacles could help researchers develop better ways to reduce those encounters. The team proposed that studying how elephants learn routes around barriers could inform strategies for human-elephant coexistence. Testing those ideas in the field would be essential before claiming that a particular approach protects crops or prevents conflict.
Article Summary: Researchers found evidence of inhibitory control, the ability to hold back an unhelpful response and switch to a successful one in seconds. The most revealing moment arrived when scientists moved the route to a fruit, forcing the animals to overcome their habit, one they had just learned.

Article Title: A Maryland factory built in 1920 once employed thousands making furniture, food and WWII rations; after sitting vacant, it has been restored as a business hub with a new $1 million oyster center
Article Text:
The Packing House’s history is closely connected to the industries that shaped the Eastern Shore.

From furniture factory to business hub

Phillips Packing Company produced food products and military rations during WW II (Photo: PRR's Cambridge Secondary Track)

$1 million project to focus on oysters

A historic factory in Cambridge, Maryland, built in 1920 has been transformed from a vacant building into a centre for businesses, entrepreneurs, food production and community programmes. The Packing House, in Dorchester County, was once linked to one of the Eastern Shore’s largest employers and is now being used for new businesses and projects connected to the region’s agricultural and maritime roots.According to Maryland Department of Commerce, the building was originally constructed as the Cambridge Furniture Company. It later became part of the Phillips Packing Company, which supported thousands of residents across Maryland’s Eastern Shore. During World War II, the company produced food products and military rations.After the building was left vacant, it has now been redeveloped by Cross Street Partners in partnership with the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy. The redevelopment has brought new activity to the historic property, which now includes office, retail and event spaces along with areas for environmental companies and non-profit organisations.The Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) has also opened its Cambridge office at the site. The redevelopment is intended to create opportunities for businesses and entrepreneurs while giving a new use to a historic building that had been sitting vacant.The Packing House’s history is closely connected to the industries that shaped the Eastern Shore. Its first use was as the Cambridge Furniture Company after it was constructed in 1920. It later became part of the Phillips Packing Company, which grew into one of the region’s largest employers.The packing company produced food products and military rations during World War II. Its operations supported thousands of people in the Eastern Shore community.The building’s latest transformation is focused on keeping it connected to the region’s existing industries. The site now supports businesses and organisations working in areas including aquaculture and environmental technologies.Maria Mougridis, project manager and community planner for DHCD, said the redevelopment of historic properties can help create stronger communities.“Revitalizing historic properties is an important part of building stronger, more sustainable communities across Maryland,” Mougridis said. “Strategic state investment can help transform vacant or overlooked locations into places where businesses can grow, entrepreneurs thrive, and communities come together,” she added.The redevelopment has therefore given the former factory a new role without removing its connection to the area’s history. Along with businesses and organisations, the property is now being used for community programming.A major part of the redevelopment is linked to oysters and environmental work. Last year, DHCD announced a $1 million state revitalisation project at the Packing House.The project is developing a centre focused on oyster processing, biotechnology laboratories, education and ecological stewardship.The work also involves the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science. With support from state funding, the centre established a regional office for Blue Oyster Environmental at the Packing House.Blue Oyster Environmental aims to become the regional leader in re-establishing the Eastern Oyster in the Chesapeake Bay ecosystem. The organisation’s work at the Packing House brings oyster-related research and environmental activities into a building that was once used for furniture production and later food and military-ration manufacturing.Dr Michael Sieracki, director and research professor at the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Sciences, said the project is intended to support oyster restoration and environmental stewardship.“Blue Oyster Environmental and UMCES remain incredibly grateful for the state’s continued support. Funding helps us turn our vision for oyster restoration and environmental stewardship into reality,” Sieracki said.He added that the continued expansion of the project would support the future of the Chesapeake Bay. “The continued expansion of this project helps to guarantee the health of our Chesapeake Bay and its future generations,” he said.
Article Summary: The Packing House, in Dorchester County, Maryland, was once linked to one of the Eastern Shore’s largest employers. The building was originally constructed as the Cambridge Furniture Company. It later became part of the Phillips Packing Company, which produced food products and military rations during World War II.

Article Title: A North Carolina land trust has saved the first 200 acres around Tuckertown Reservoir after 1,400 donors joined the campaign; another 3,800 privately owned acres remain at risk of sale and development
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

The first 200 acres are now protected

Why the shoreline is important

Thousands of acres are still at risk

A campaign built around keeping access open

The next phase is much bigger

A conservation campaign in North Carolina has secured the first 200 acres of land around Tuckertown Reservoir, preserving public access to a stretch of shoreline and forest that has been available to outdoor users for decades. The Three Rivers Land Trust (TRLT), which is leading the Save Tuckertown campaign, announced the completion of the first acquisition in August 2026. According to the organisation, more than 1,400 grassroots donors contributed to the effort, with donations coming from across the US and beyond. The first tract will ultimately be transferred to the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission and remain part of the state’s public gamelands.The 200-acre acquisition, however, represents only the first phase of a much larger conservation effort. TRLT says about 3,800 additional acres surrounding Tuckertown Reservoir remain at stake. The land has historically been privately owned by Alcoa but has been enrolled in the North Carolina Gamelands Program, allowing public recreational access. The conservation group is now seeking to acquire additional parcels before they can potentially be sold for development.The first part of the campaign has now moved from fundraising to a completed land purchase. Three Rivers Land Trust (TRLT) acquired 200 acres around Tuckertown Reservoir and plans to transfer the property to the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission. The land will remain available through the state's public gamelands system rather than being closed off for private use.That distinction matters because the property has not historically functioned like an ordinary piece of private land. Although the surrounding acreage has been privately owned, it has been enrolled in the North Carolina Gamelands Program, allowing members of the public to use it for recreation. The campaign attracted support from a surprisingly wide area. TRLT says more than 1,400 grassroots donors contributed, with donations coming from every US state, Guam, Canada and Europe.The fundraising effort also received support from outdoor companies onX and MeatEater, which participated in a matching campaign. The North Carolina Wildlife Habitat Foundation contributed $40,000 toward the priority tract, with the contribution matched by the two companies. For TRLT, the response was a sign that the concern over Tuckertown extends beyond the people who live immediately around the reservoir.The land surrounding Tuckertown Reservoir is valuable for reasons that go beyond public access. The forested properties provide habitat for wildlife and help maintain a natural buffer along the reservoir. Keeping large portions of that landscape intact also means the shoreline is less likely to be transformed by development. There is a history behind the current campaign as well. Some land around Tuckertown has already been protected through previous conservation efforts. TRLT points out that the remaining properties were not covered by a 2007 relicensing settlement that resulted in other Tuckertown-area land being conserved. That has left a substantial amount of privately owned property in a different position.The land trust is now working to prevent those remaining parcels from being sold and potentially developed. Its concern is particularly relevant because of the area's proximity to several population centres. TRLT notes that nearly 80% of North Carolina's population lives within 100 miles of the Tuckertown lands. If the properties change hands and are developed, public access to parts of the shoreline could become more limited.The 200-acre purchase is only the beginning of the Save Tuckertown campaign. TRLT estimates that another 3,800 acres around the reservoir remain at risk of being sold. The organisation is seeking to acquire those properties gradually, depending on funding and opportunities to purchase the land. One of the next major targets is an approximately 800-acre tract. The property includes more than four miles of shoreline and a mature hardwood forest. It also has views of Tuckertown Reservoir from Highway 49. The land trust says properties such as this could be sold at any time. If they are purchased for private development, the character of the shoreline could change considerably, along with the way the public uses the area.TRLT's plan is to step in where possible, purchase the properties and eventually transfer them to the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission. The goal is to keep the land within the public gamelands system rather than simply placing it under another form of private conservation ownership.That public-access element is central to the project. Conservation does not always mean that land becomes public. In this case, however, TRLT is deliberately pursuing a route that can keep people on the land. Once properties are acquired, they can remain available for public recreation while arrangements are made for their eventual transfer.The land trust has followed a similar approach elsewhere in North Carolina. According to TRLT, it has helped move more than 8,000 acres into public ownership, including properties around High Rock Lake and along the eastern shoreline of Tuckertown. The first 200 acres at Tuckertown now form another part of that effort.For the moment, the campaign has a clear achievement to point to: 200 acres have been secured with help from more than 1,400 donors. But the much larger figure is still ahead. With about 3,800 privately owned acres remaining at risk, TRLT's work at Tuckertown is far from finished. The organisation will need to continue raising money and finding opportunities to purchase individual properties. Each successful acquisition could keep another section of shoreline, forest and recreational land from changing hands.For those who already use Tuckertown Reservoir, the first 200 acres offer some certainty. The wider landscape, however, will depend on what happens with the thousands of acres that remain.
Article Summary: Three Rivers Land Trust (TRLT) acquired 200 acres around Tuckertown Reservoir and plans to transfer the property to the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission. The land will remain available through the state's public gamelands system rather than being closed off for private use. Another 3,800 acres around the reservoir remain at risk of being sold.

Article Title: $26,000 to fight for Russia: How Moscow recruits Americans via TikTok and Telegram
Article Text:
File photo: Russian President Vladimir Putin arrives for a wreath-laying ceremony surrounded by Russian military personnels

US citizens joining Russia's war

Russia is increasingly turning to foreign recruits to replenish its forces fighting in Ukraine, with at least 18 Americans identified as having joined the Russian military, according to Ukrainian officials cited by the New York Post. US recruits are reportedly being offered a signing bonus of about $26,000, along with a monthly salary.The recruitment is being driven through a network of agents who use platforms including Facebook, TikTok and Telegram to find potential recruits. Ukrainian officials said recruiters can earn money for each person they bring in, with some reportedly receiving about $24,000 per recruit as well as a share of the recruit’s salary.The effort extends far beyond Americans. Ukrainian security officials have identified nearly 29,000 foreigners from 135 countries fighting for Russia, although the actual number could be higher. Amnesty International has separately documented deceptive and exploitative recruitment practices targeting foreign nationals, including promises of civilian jobs, high salaries, legal status or Russian citizenship.One of those recruited was Seth William Baker, a former US Marine from Gilbert, Arizona. Baker, who had served as a lance corporal and worked as a bulk fuel specialist, was 23 when he was killed on the frontlines in Ukraine, around three months after signing up.Baker had joined the Marines at 18 but was later discharged after refusing the military's Covid-19 vaccine mandate. He subsequently became involved with Russian propaganda online before travelling to Russia.In a recording made from a Russian bunker, Baker said the vaccine mandate had been one of the factors behind his decision to leave the US military and join Russia's war effort.Vitaliy Matvienko, who heads Ukraine's state-backed project encouraging Russian soldiers to surrender, described Baker's case as typical of the people Russia's recruitment network seeks out. He said Russia had turned foreign recruitment into an “entire industry” as it struggles to replace battlefield losses.Baker is not the only American identified as having fought for Russia.Michael Gloss, 21, the son of a former CIA official, was killed while fighting in Ukraine in April 2024. Ukrainian intelligence has also identified 17 other Americans who had enlisted in the Russian military.Another case involves former Massachusetts city councillor Wilmer Puello-Mota, who left the US while facing a child sexual-abuse-related case and later joined Russian forces. He was wounded by shrapnel in Ukraine in August.Derek Huffman, 47, moved his family to Russia and later signed up for the military, according to the report. He had previously criticised what he described as LGBTQ “indoctrination” in the US and said he wanted to earn respect and Russian citizenship.Matvienko said foreign recruits serve a dual purpose for Moscow: they provide additional manpower while also allowing Russia to portray Americans and other foreigners fighting alongside its troops as evidence of international support for its war.Foreign recruits can also be easier for Russia to absorb politically when they are killed, he said, because their deaths do not necessarily generate the same reaction inside Russian society as the deaths of Russian soldiers.The recruitment comes as Russia continues to sustain heavy battlefield losses. Ukrainian officials cited by the New York Post estimated that Russia was suffering tens of thousands of casualties each month and increasingly relying on foreign nationals to help fill its ranks.
Article Summary: US recruits are reportedly being offered a signing bonus of about $26,000, along with a monthly salary. Ukrainian officials said recruiters can earn money for each person they bring in. Some reportedly receive about $24,000 per recruit as well as a share of the recruit’s salary.

Article Title: Camp Mystic owners seek to sell the century-old Texas girls’ camp after the 2025 flood; the bankruptcy plan puts its entire 749-acre riverfront property up for auction while families of victims fight
Article Text:
Camp Mystic, LLC

Natural Fountains Properties, Inc.

Mystic Camps Family Partnership, Ltd.

Mystic Camps Management, LLC

Camp Mystic has been in the news since 2025. The camp was the site of a catastrophic flash flooding along the Guadalupe River in Texas on July 4, 2025 that led to the death of 28 people, including 25 young campers, two teenage counselors and the camp's co-owner and director, Dick Eastland. A year later, the owners of the camp have proposed selling off the riverfront property as part of a bankruptcy plan, with hopes that a buyer will preserve the camp's "historic mission" following the harrowing incident.The century-old private Christian girls' camp filed a Chapter 11 bankruptcy reorganisation plan on September 25, 2025, with debts estimated between $10 million and $50 million, stating it would auction off 749 acres it owns along with other assets. The camp’s bankruptcy proposal would have to be approved by U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Christopher M. Lopez.The camp has been owned by the Eastland Family for decades and initially sought to reopen this summer. However, they faced fierce opposition from victims' families and some state lawmakers, lawsuits and legislative investigations that went wrong. A buyer would likely get a portion of the camp frozen in time. Families of the victims have fought to stop any demolition of damaged cabins and buildings and to stop repairs as part of their lawsuits.Under the proposed plan, virtually all Camp Mystic assets would be sold through a court-supervised sale process. The proceeds would be preserved and distributed to creditors, which include the families of the campers and counsellors who died. Other creditors include unsecured creditors and families who made deposits for the 2026 season before Camp Mystic withdrew its license application. Additionally, per the filing, insurance coverage would first cover those claims, and if that coverage doesn't fully cover the claims, the families would share the remaining funds with the other unsecured creditors. All creditors, including the families who have sued Camp Mystic over the deaths, will have a chance to respond to the plan.Edward S. Eastland, a member of the family that owns the camp, was listed as the camp's authorised representative in the filing. The corporation behind the camp is represented by a Dallas attorney.A total of four companies are listed as affiliated entities in the filing:“The Eastlands are now attempting to determine the future of the Camp Mystic property, but the victims’ families, including my clients, will fight to protect their rights and ensure any sale is fair and transparent,” said Tim Ferguson, attorney for the family of 8-year-old Mary Grace Baker, one of the campers who died. “The Bakers intend to continue fighting for answers, accountability and justice for their daughter,” Ferguson said.The bankruptcy plan said the owners expect a purchaser would be backed by a group of families that support the camp. “Nothing in the plan requires any buyer to operate the property as a camp,” the filing said, “but the plan states an express preference, in determining the highest or otherwise best bid, for a buyer that will maintain the historic mission of the camp.”The river surged over its banks in the pre-dawn hours of July 4, 2025. At least 136 people were killed along a several-mile stretch of the river. State investigations and court filings revealed that camp leadership received a life-threatening flash flood alert on their phones around 1:15 am, but delayed beginning evacuations for roughly 45 minutes. Moreover, a probe by state lawmakers determined the young and inexperienced counsellors lacked emergency training, and the camp did not effectively utilise its alert systems, including its PA network, as water levels rose. It said an earlier decision to evacuate could have saved every life. Most of the victims were under age 10, and some were attending camp for the first time.Earlier this month, state police investigators sought search warrants for the electronic communications of the camp’s owners, saying they could provide evidence of manslaughter, negligent homicide, child abandonment or other crimes. No charges have been brought forward as of yet.
Article Summary: Camp Mystic was the site of a catastrophic flash flooding on July 4, 2025. 28 people died, including 25 young campers, two teenage counselors and the camp's co-owner and director, Dick Eastland. A year later, the owners of the camp have proposed selling off the riverfront property as part of a bankruptcy plan.

Article Title: Russia backs India's claim to UNSC seat, firmly shuts door on Germany & Japan
Article Text:
Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly (Photo: Reuters).

Russia on Saturday backed a permanent seat for India and Brazil on the United Nations Security Council, while strongly opposing the same for Western countries.During his speech at the General Assembly, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said no additional seats at the UNSC should be given to Western countries, especially to Germany and the US ally, Japan.Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India’s bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council . Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.Lavrov has previously argued that the current composition no longer reflects today’s global balance and explicitly endorsed India, alongside Brazil, for permanent membership.This support was reiterated in the 2026 BRICS New Delhi Declaration, with China and Russia backing India and Brazil for a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.Lavrov accused the West of continuously pumping weapons into Ukraine while helping target drones and missiles at Russia's civilians and civilian infrastructure.He also mentioned that Europe raised an anti-Moscow regime in Kyivv, in order to control the Russian influence."To pursue a utopian goal of containing Russia, the West dismantled the European security system and cultivated a Russophobic regime in Kyiv," he said, while warning the Western nations of "consequences".He further accused Europe of doing everything to block a peaceful settlement with Ukraine and disrupt negotiation prospects favoured by many, including the Trump administration.Lavrov claimed several EU leaders of being infected with racial superiority, encouraging the rise of what he called Ukrainian Nazism.The Russian foreign minister said the UN’s core principles were being put at risk, with the West overlooking the spread of Nazism in Ukraine.
Article Summary: Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India's bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Article Title: Pentagon data hack exposes 3 million people's information as FBI probes another data leak
Article Text:
The Pentagon breach comes as the FBI is responding to a separate incident involving its jobs website.

What information was exposed

FBI also deals with jobs portal breach

A security breach at a Pentagon personnel database exposed sensitive information linked to more than 3 million people, including military personnel, civilian employees and others connected to the US defence establishment, according to a US defence official.The breach affected 2.76 million living people and 294,000 deceased individuals, the official said. The exposed information included Social Security numbers and details about the jobs held by military and civilian personnel. The nature of the information has raised concerns about the potential national security implications.The unauthorised access took place between October 2025 and July 2026, when the vulnerability was discovered and fixed.“A Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) information system experienced unauthorized access of personally identifiable information by a small number of unauthorized users between October 2025 and July 2026. Upon discovery, DMDC immediately remediated the vulnerability,” the official said.The Defense Manpower Data Center is one of the Pentagon's main systems for maintaining personnel records. Its databases cover active-duty and reserve troops, civilian employees, contractors, retirees, veterans and military family members.The agency holds more than 60 million personnel records. Military Times first reported the breach last week.Defence officials said there is currently no evidence that the exposed information has been misused. They are offering identity protection and credit monitoring services to people whose information was affected.The Pentagon breach comes as the FBI is responding to a separate incident involving its jobs website, FBIJobs.gov.The FBI sent employees a notice on Friday after a threat actor claimed it had obtained information including employees' names, home addresses, personal and work contact details, Social Security numbers, dates of birth and emergency contact information, sources told ABC News.The bureau is treating the situation as though the personal information of all FBI employees may have been compromised. Employees whose information was affected have started receiving notifications, while the FBI has stressed that the compromised system was unclassified.The hacking group ShinyHunters later claimed it would not publish the data. In a statement to the New York Times and 404 Media on Monday, the group said its actions were intended as a marketing campaign rather than an attempt to extort money."Since the very beginning of this event we have unequivocally and assiduously emphasised this is NOT extortion, this is NOT ransom, this is NOT financially motivated," the statement said. “This was all a marketing campaign to protect our business and actively combat disinformation. If we made this statement normally then this much attention to our words and intentions would’ve never been this widespread."The FBI has advised potentially affected employees to remain alert and avoid responding to suspicious calls. Internal briefings are also planned for those affected.According to the warning described to ABC News, employees have been told not to speak to the media and to call 911 if journalists are "trespassing".
Article Summary: The breach affected 2.76 million living people and 294,000 deceased individuals. The exposed information included Social Security numbers and details about the jobs held by military and civilian personnel. The FBI is treating the situation as though the personal information of all FBI employees may have been compromised.

Article Title: 49 killed in Myanmar as junta carries out airstrike at rebel-controlled Rakhine region
Article Text:
Aftermath of a Myanmar military airstrike.

Arakan army threatens retaliation

Poll Vote & Share your view Should international intervention be considered in the Myanmar conflict? Yes, to protect civilians No, the conflict should be resolved internally 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: An airstrike by Myanmar's military near a market in rebel-controlled territory in western Rakhine state killed at least 49 people and injured 58 others on Monday, according to the Arakan army and a rescue official.The attack took place in Kyauktaw township, about 340 km (210 miles) west of Mandalay, Myanmar’s second-largest city. The area is controlled by the Arakan Army, a powerful ethnic armed group operating in Rakhine.According to the Arakan Army, a fighter jet dropped two bombs near a local market around noon, killing vendors, shoppers and pedestrians. Of the 58 people injured, 22 were in critical condition, the group said.Wai Hun Aung, a senior rescue official in Rakhine, confirmed the casualties to The Associated Press, citing rescue workers at the scene. He said the market was the region’s main wholesale centre and attracted traders and shoppers from across the state.“This is one of the most severe airstrikes in Rakhine,” he said.Photos and videos shared on social media showed buildings on fire, damaged vehicles and parts of a nearby bridge destroyed.However TOI could not independently verify them.The Arakan Army said the attack was the latest in a series of deadly airstrikes by Myanmar’s military against pro-democracy resistance forces and ethnic armed groups across the country.The group said it "will take effective retaliatory measures soon against the individuals and organisations directly responsible for the attacks involving deliberate airstrikes that have caused mass casualties.”The Myanmar military did not immediately comment on Monday’s attack. It has previously said its airstrikes target legitimate military positions and accused resistance groups of terrorism.Myanmar has been engulfed in conflict since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi on February 1, 2021.The military’s crackdown on widespread protests against the coup pushed many opponents to take up arms, triggering fighting across large parts of the country.The Arakan Army is the armed wing of a movement seeking greater autonomy for Rakhine’s ethnic minority from Myanmar’s central government. It launched an offensive in Rakhine in November 2023 and has since captured a strategically important regional military headquarters and 14 of the state’s 17 townships.Fighting in Rakhine has also disrupted trade routes and worsened food shortages as the military imposed severe restrictions on movement and commerce. In December, a military airstrike on a hospital in Rakhine’s Mrauk-U township killed at least 34 people and wounded 80 others.
Article Summary: The attack took place in Kyauktaw township, about 340 km (210 miles) west of Mandalay. The area is controlled by the Arakan Army, a powerful ethnic armed group. Of the 58 people injured, 22 were in critical condition, the group said.

Article Title: In 2024, 75-year-old Iowa farmer Evie Haupt said three wind turbines on her 160 acres were bringing in about $35,000 a year while using under 3 acres and had helped reduce $350,000 in farm debt to $67
Article Text:
A financial lifeline for rural landowners

The explosive expansion of Iowa wind power

Addressing local pushback and debate

On a 160-acre farm in central Iowa, three tall wind turbines quietly rise above the fields. Each turbine uses less than an acre of land, but together they provide an annual income that has changed the financial future of 75-year-old farmer Evie Haupt. According to a CBS News report by Janet Shamlian and Alicia Hastey, Haupt earns about $35,000 each year by leasing part of her land for the wind turbines. The income rises with inflation and has helped her pay down a $350,000 farm debt left after her husband died a decade ago. Her remaining debt is now $67,000. For many family farms across the United States, extra sources of income have become important lifelines. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects farm profits to fall by 25 per cent, as farmers face higher costs, changing crop prices and unpredictable weather. Adding wind power to traditional farming can provide steady income and help protect farmers from financial shocks.Farm debt can leave families with difficult choices, including selling land that has been in the family for generations. Haupt faced this situation after her husband died and left her with hundreds of thousands of dollars in farm debt.Payments from the wind turbines provided her with a regular source of income that she could use to repay the loans. Each turbine takes up less than an acre, allowing Haupt to continue farming most of her 160 acres. This means the same land provides her with two sources of income while only a small portion is used for the turbines. The payments can also increase over time because the contracts include inflation adjustments, helping landowners manage rising prices and other costs. For Haupt, the arrangement has made a significant difference. She has now paid off more than 80% of her farm debt while continuing to use the land for farming.Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Iowa had only a few hundred wind turbines 20 years ago. Today, it has more than 6,000, producing about 60 per cent of the state's energy. Across the United States, more than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Federal energy officials also say current U.S. wind power cuts carbon emissions by an amount equal to taking 73 million passenger vehicles off the road. Attorney Kathy Law, who grew up on a farm and married a farmer, has helped place nearly half of Iowa's wind turbines. Her work in energy law grew from her own family's experience with farming. Law wanted to study law while she was in high school, but the severe farm crisis of the 1980s kept her home to help with the family farm. She later went to law school in her forties. She graduated on the same day her son finished high school and later served as president of the Iowa Wind Energy Association for three years. "From my farm background, I think I can talk their talk and have conversations with landowners that are interested in having wind turbines on their property," Law told CBS News.The rapid growth of wind power in rural communities has also brought opposition in some counties. Local critics say wind turbines can change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats. Law believes landowners should be able to decide what happens on their property. "Nobody's requiring them to put that on their farms or on their land," Law said during her interview with CBS News. "We want to be able to put turbines on our land and receive those benefits. " Haupt has a similar view of the changes to her farm. While she remains attached to traditional farming, she sees clean energy as an important step for rural communities. "I look at it as progress," Haupt told CBS News. "I think we can't stand in the way of progress." For Haupt, giving up a very small part of her land to produce electricity makes sense for her finances and for the wider community. "I need to give up one or two acres of my land so that I can generate a commodity that we all use every day, and we all want to use more of it every day," Haupt said. "So I'm happy to be able to be a part of that generation."
Article Summary: Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. More than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating in the U.S. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Critics say wind turbines change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats.

Article Title: Since 1977, a photographer has kept returning to America’s changing inner cities; his decades-long record captured Harlem’s decline and transformation
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image. Credits - Gemini

A camera and a sociologist

Twenty-six images of one address

AI-generated representative image. Credits - Gemini

Breaking up, then reshaping differently

Reviews in History

Photographs typically capture a moment. A single shot can depict a street on a specific afternoon, but it cannot reveal the street's subsequent developments. A few documentary photographers have attempted to address the issue by repeatedly returning to the same location, which is a methodical and somewhat obstinate approach.One of them is Camilo José Vergara. He has spent nearly five decades photographing America's changing cities, and the Library of Congress holds his photograph collection, with more than 5,000 chosen best pictures, held in its Prints and Pictures Division. The library notes that his photographs show how areas can fall into decay and, in some cases, come back to life because he returns to the same vantage points over long periods.Born in Santiago, Chile, in 1944 to a rich family, Vergara's family was broke by the time he was fifteen. He moved to the United States and earned a bachelor's degree in sociology from the University of Notre Dame in 1968, followed by a master's degree in sociology from Columbia University in 1977. That background influenced his attitude. He has said his mission was to document the damage and violence that had affected New York during a period of urban crisis.In the early 1970s, when he first picked up a camera, he concentrated on people living in damaged areas.With time he turned his attention to the buildings and streets themselves, which he came to consider as a more reliable record of the choices made by residents and city officials over the long haul. His projects now span New York, Newark, Camden, Detroit, Chicago, Gary, Los Angeles and Richmond, California, among others.The narrative of 65 East 125th Street is told by the National Endowment for the Humanities, which honoured Vergara with the National Humanities Medal in 2012. It is located on the main Harlem artery between Madison and Park Avenues. Vergara started shooting it in 1977, and his first image shows crimson double doors, cocktail glasses painted on the front, and a sign for the Purple Manor.The changes are coming fast. By 1980 the doors were black and white, and a restaurant advertised fish and chips for $2.25. The building was a bargain variety store in 1981. Then it became a smoking shop, a unisex boutique, a beauty shop, a clothing store and a Sleepy's Mattress Store. In the final picture of the 26-image sequence, taken in 2009, the space was for rent.Vergara positioned himself in the same spot for each picture and used equivalent cameras and lenses so the images could be compared directly. Multiply that discipline across dozens of locations, and you have a kind of visual data set. The 26-image sequence is one part of Vergara's broader long-term documentation of Harlem and other American cities.Vergara’s Harlem is a place of wreckage and rebirth. A review innotes that new and restored buildings are attracting more affluent Black and Latino residents, along with some white residents. It also notes that chain businesses now line much of West 125th Street, while national retailers and new condominiums have displaced some long-standing businesses and residents.Researchers at Rutgers' humanities institute make a similar argument. They note that many symptoms of ghetto life, including physical deterioration and social dysfunction, emerge in the book, but so do signs of metamorphosis, some of them striking. They also point out the discomfort that gentrification has created in a long area called the capital of Black America.The Library of Congress study guides lay out the balance clearly. Some communities degrade as long-established businesses give way to vacant shopfronts, graffiti and garbage, while others gentrify. Vergara also captures the street life that persists through it all, such as stoop parties, parades and paintings.Invincible Cities, an interactive website supported by Rutgers University and the Ford Foundation, makes Vergara's time-sequenced photographs from Harlem, Richmond and Camden available online. The patience of his record is its strength. Vergara does not tell readers whether the changes are positive or negative; he simply documents how places change over time, leaving the interpretation to viewers.
Article Summary: Camilo José Vergara has spent nearly five decades photographing America's changing cities. The Library of Congress holds his photograph collection, with more than 5,000 chosen best pictures, held in its Prints and Pictures Division. His projects now span New York, Newark, Camden, Detroit, Chicago, Gary, Los Angeles and Richmond, California, among others.

Article Title: Between 1907 and 1928, a Kansas retiree built a home and garden from concrete, leaving more than 150 sculptures now preserved as the Garden of Eden
Article Text:
The Garden of Eden in Lucas, Kansas, showing Samuel P. Dinsmoor’s limestone cabin surrounded by his elaborate network of concrete sculptures depicting biblical, political and social themes. Credits - gardenofedenlucas.org

A stone log cabin

Concrete with a mission

Samuel P. Dinsmoor’s Garden of Eden in Lucas, Kansas, featuring the sculptural trees and concrete figures surrounding his unusual limestone “log” cabin. Credits - Wikipedia

Reclaimed from neglect

Samuel Perry Dinsmoor was a former teacher and Union Army veteran who, after moving from his farm into the little town of Lucas in central Kansas, chose to spend his retirement building a cabin, a garden and a statement about the world. According to the Kansas Historical Society , Dinsmoor created more than 150 concrete sculptures there, many of which reflect his religious views and Populist politics. The site is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and he worked on it from 1907 to 1928. It is now called the Garden of Eden and is considered one of the best examples of grassroots art in the United States.Dinsmoor was born in Ohio in 1843, according to the Kansas Historical Society. He enlisted in the Union Army in 1862, served three years and saw 18 major battles, including Gettysburg. He then taught school in Illinois for five terms before turning to farming. In 1888 he moved to Russell County, Kansas, spent a spell in Nebraska and was back in Russell County by 1891. He retired from farming in 1905, moved into Lucas and bought a quarter of a block, and that is where the Garden of Eden began.The showpiece was a stone log cabin that was not made of logs at all.Dinsmoor used local post rock limestone, a stone that got its name because farmers carved it into fence posts on a prairie that lacked timber. The Kohler Foundation describes an eleven-room cabin built from that limestone. Dinsmoor's own description mentions a private light plant under the back porch, and local tradition holds that it was the first cabin in Lucas to have electricity.According to the Kansas Historical Society, Dinsmoor used 113 tons of cement on the garden, and this is where the story moves from architecture to argument. The Kohler Foundation says his sculptures reflect both his Populist ideas and his religious convictions, and both organisations count roughly 150 pieces.According to the National Register nomination, many of the statues sit on concrete trees, some as high as forty feet. A tableau depicts a doctor, a lawyer, a priest, and a banker crucifying labour. Another has a Goddess of Liberty. Life-size representations of Adam and Eve welcomed tourists, though local politicians soon demanded they wear concrete loincloths. Dinsmoor even rigged a speaking tube so he could address curious passersby through the mouth of an angel. He also had a mausoleum erected for himself on the grounds, and visitors can still see him in a coffin with a glass top. Building the garden was demanding work, and Dinsmoor built it to last, molding each figure over steel and chicken wire.Dinsmoor died in 1932. His wife sold the property to pay her taxes, and the garden went to seed. It sat neglected until it was bought and reopened as an attraction in the late 1960s, and it joined the National Register of Historic Places on April 28, 1977. In 2012, the Kohler Foundation sponsored a substantial renovation. Crews stripped away vines and trees, wiped away years of moss and mould, and revealed the original stained concrete. Some figures were also freed of the concrete loincloths the community had once demanded. The Kohler Foundation says the garden now draws more than 10,000 visitors a year to a community of fewer than 500 people.Its meaning has also broadened. The National Trust for Historic Preservation describes a stone log cabin surrounded by tall concrete sculptures that protest against bank trusts and monopolies. The trust adds that Dinsmoor's populist vision has been at the heart of Lucas since 1909, just two years after he began building.The Garden of Eden is near the corner of Kansas and Second Streets in Lucas, along the Post Rock Scenic Byway. There are guided tours that discuss the tales behind the sculptures, and opening hours vary by season, so it's worth checking the official Garden of Eden website before heading out. Dinsmoor wanted people to stop and look, and more than a century later they still do.
Article Summary: Samuel Perry Dinsmoor was a former teacher and Union Army veteran who, after moving from his farm into the little town of Lucas in central Kansas, chose to spend his retirement building a cabin, a garden and a statement about the world. The site is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and he worked on it from 1907 to 1928. It is now called the Garden of Eden and is considered one of the best examples of grassroots art in the United States.

Article Title: From 1912 to 1945, a New York landowner planted up to 55,000 trees a year; the experiments helped shape America's tree-planting programmes
Article Text:
Portrait of Franklin D. Roosevelt alongside Springwood Estate at Franklin D. Roosevelt National Historic Site. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

A crop not a view

Trees that earned their keep

The grave of Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt is located in Hyde Park, New York. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

Hyde Park to national policy

Most people will likely cite sailing or stamp collecting when asked what Franklin D. Roosevelt did to unwind. Foresters typically respond differently. The record demonstrates that Roosevelt took his self-described status as a tree farmer seriously. He spent most of his adult life transforming steep slopes and dilapidated fields into functioning woods on the family property at Hyde Park in the Hudson Valley of New York.People are surprised by the scale. Roosevelt purchased his first saplings in 1912, the year he was appointed chairman of the New York Senate's Forestry Committee, according to the National Park Service . He would plant close to half a million trees over the following three decades. By the 1930s the estate was taking in somewhere between 20,000 and 55,000 new trees a year, and the habit continued until his death in 1945.Behind those numbers sits a bigger question. Was the endeavour a wealthy man's hobby, or something closer to a field experiment that shaped how America thought about reforestation? The evidence leans towards the second.Eventually, the estate swelled to about 1,600 acres. Some 800 acres were native woodlands, 400 acres were orchards, pastures and tilled fields, and the remaining 400 acres were set aside for Roosevelt's tree planting, with about 250 of them carrying established plantations by 1943.The difference was his approach to those plantations. The park agency says he saw his woodlots as a crop rather than scenery, and he wanted the property to stay productive for the long term.He did not labour alone. In 1930 he teamed up with Nelson C. Brown, a professor of forestry at the New York State College of Forestry at Syracuse University. Between 1930 and 1933, the college established 36 plantations with roughly 88,600 trees. After 1933, according to the National Park Service, Brown served for twelve more years as Roosevelt's unofficial and unpaid forest manager, helping him expand the programme and begin Christmas tree production on a large scale.A neighbour had shown what was possible. The conservation group Scenic Hudson cites the railway magnate Archibald Rogers, who planted a tree farm on his Hyde Park estate and gradually trimmed it as the trees matured. Roosevelt learned from the example and then pressed on, with a trained forester at his side.Some plots were purely experimental or demonstration plantings, which turned the estate into what the park service describes as a learning laboratory that gave others data. In 1943 Brown reported the results in the Journal of Forestry , noting that the family woodlands then held 800 acres of natural growth and 250 acres of plantations. The most recent felling had supplied oak and shipbuilding timber for the war effort, a reminder that a gentleman's wood had become a real source of wartime material.Christmas trees were something of a hallmark crop. Roosevelt sent trees from Hyde Park to Winston Churchill, and the NPS archives hold memos to the estate manager, William Plog, about the 1943 Christmas tree gifts. It was a telling detail, and it showed how seriously the operation was run. There were managers, records and a market. He was not simply a man with a shovel.To imply that one estate designed America’s tree-planting schemes is going too far. Roosevelt had numerous advisers, and forestry science was rapidly advancing over these decades. But he arrived at the White House fully convinced, from his own soil, that planting trees at scale was practicable, measurable and worth public funds. The best representation of that philosophy is the Civilian Conservation Corps, created in 1933.Let New York's own records tell the tale. The Department of Environmental Conservation says Roosevelt had a specific interest in forestry and began planting his estate with seedlings from the state tree nursery in 1912. The Depression cut state financing for tree planting, but the Corps revived the scheme, planting millions of saplings in barren soil and giving jobs to thousands of young men. Work slowed again during the war years, from 1941 to 1945.The Hyde Park plantings are a handy reminder that big conservation movements often start with someone testing an idea on their own land. Roosevelt planted hundreds of thousands of trees, kept detailed records with professional help, and then carried the same confidence into national policy. Many of those trees still stand in the Hudson Valley today.
Article Summary: Franklin D. Roosevelt spent most of his adult life transforming steep slopes and dilapidated fields into functioning woods. He purchased his first saplings in 1912, the year he was appointed chairman of the New York Senate's Forestry Committee. By the 1930s the estate was taking in somewhere between 20,000 and 55,000 new trees a year, and the habit continued until his death in 1945.

Article Title: In 1907, Frank O. Lowden began planting trees on bare land; over several decades, 500,000 trees grew into today’s 2,291-acre Lowden-Miller State Forest
Article Text:
Frank O. Lowden, who served as governor of Illinois from 1917 to 1921, appears in a representative image. Credits - Wikipedia, Wikimedia Commons

Stubborn concept and sandy earth

A forest becomes a classroom

Representative image. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

Family land and public forest

In the Rock River Valley of northern Illinois, about three miles south of the town of Oregon, a forest exists largely because one man kept planting. The individual was Frank O. Lowden, governor of Illinois from 1917 to 1921. Before and after his years in the statehouse, he treated his land as a decades-long reforestation experiment. According to the Illinois Department of Natural Resources , Lowden or his team planted an estimated 500,000 trees over several decades. That land is now Lowden-Miller State Forest in Ogle County, a public woodland of 2,291 acres that anyone can wander through, though the state only bought it in 1992 and 1993.The acreage that Lowden owned along the Rock River was never just farmland. It combined native hardwoods with pasture and patches of sandy soil that were poor producers when cropped. Instead of fighting the dirt, Lowden began experimenting with white pines and other species to see what would grow well. The state's records place his earliest white pine plantings before 1910, and they are believed to be the oldest in Illinois.Those early plantings date from the same years as his time in Congress, from 1906 to 1911, long before anyone thought of him as a governor.His logic was practical as well as emotional. He believed in reforestation to slow soil erosion, a major concern on loose, sandy slopes over a river. Trees would hold the earth and, in time, become timber.He named the site Sinnissippi Forest, a word from American Indian languages that is commonly rendered “rocky river” or “troubled waters.” The name was passed down with the family for generations. But before the property could become a public asset, someone had to figure out if all those plantings actually worked.In 1938 Lowden invited the University of Illinois’s newly created forestry department to study the expanding forest. That invitation was important well beyond his acres. The Illinois Department of Natural Resources says nearly 80 percent of all data on Illinois hardwood forest growth has come from Sinnissippi, and the forest still serves as a field laboratory for the university.That is a striking claim for a single private estate, and it helps explain why the plantings matter. Records that follow tree growth over many years are rare, because they take decades to build and a short experiment never can. A stand planted in the early 1900s and measured for most of a century tells foresters a great deal about how a forest grows. The US Forest Service defines the eastern white pine as among the most rapidly growing conifers of northern forests, an excellent choice for reforestation, and one of the more widely planted trees in America. Its native range reaches northern Illinois, which suited what Lowden was trying to do on his sandy soils.As the forest matured, commercial use and scientific study grew alongside it. The family's Christmas tree business began in 1948 and ran until 2009, according to the state. In 1955, Sinnissippi Forest became the first tree farm in Illinois. The land that had failed to grow crops became a forest used for timber, research and public recreation.By the early 1990s, Lowden’s grandsons owned the estate. In June 1992 the state bought 1,186 acres from Warren P. Miller and his wife Nancy, and another 1,039 acres followed in 1993 from his brother Phillip Lowden Miller and his wife Bonnie. The family said that by selling to the state rather than seeing the land subdivided, they kept it an actively managed forest. The combined property became Lowden-Miller State Forest, which the state says now totals 2,291 acres. Visitors can see bluffs that rise 120 feet along 3.5 miles of riverfront, where hardwoods grow among the pines, according to the state. The forest sits across the Rock River from Castle Rock State Park, which oversees its daily operations.Politics never held him as tightly as his land did. He left Congress in 1911, and when he ran for governor in 1916, he said he wanted only one term because he would rather return to his farm and forest, as the Illinois Department of Natural Resources tells it. In 1921, he left office and returned to the trees. The result is a public forest that grew from one person's private plan. Its 2,291 acres are open to anyone with walking shoes, and the estimated 500,000 trees that Lowden planted or oversaw are the reason it exists.
Article Summary: Frank O. Lowden, who served as governor of Illinois from 1917 to 1921, treated his land as a decades-long reforestation experiment. According to the Illinois Department of Natural Resources, Lowden or his team planted an estimated 500,000 trees over several decades. That land is now Lowden-Miller State Forest in Ogle County, a public woodland of 2,291 acres that anyone can wander through.

Article Title: Minnesota has picked a nearly 57-acre site for a $1 billion horticulture world's fair expected to draw millions; after the six-month Expo ends, the land is planned to become a permanent mixed-use dist
Article Text:
Rendering of the proposed US Pavilion for Expo 2031 in Minnesota. (Minnesota Star Tribune photo)

Expo around horticulture and 'Human/Nature'

Organisers expect development to continue

Aerial view of Lakeville, a suburb of the Twin Cities in Minnesota.

Lakeville residents question project

Traffic and public outreach

Minnesota has selected Lakeville as the planned host city for Expo 2031, a six-month international exhibition focused on horticulture. According to Minnesota Star Tribune, organisers have signed a purchase agreement for nearly 57 acres of land near Interstate 35 and County Road 70, with the event expected to attract millions of visitors.The Expo is scheduled to run from May to October 2031. It would be the first A1 International Horticultural Exhibition to be held in the United States. These exhibitions bring together international pavilions, gardens and programmes focused on horticulture and related themes.The event is being planned on a much larger scale than the 57-acre parcel already secured. Wendy Meadley, CEO and board chair of Expo 2031, said the remaining land needed for the project would be acquired through methods including leasing. The total area involved is expected to be about 180 acres.Expo 2031 is being planned around the theme “Human/Nature”. The exhibition is expected to include international and national pavilions, gardens and other visitor attractions.Plans for the Lakeville site currently include a 200-room hotel, a 1,300-space parking structure, an Expo Hall and a community welcome centre. The site is also planned to have a media studio and a 1,500-person amphitheatre.Another proposed feature is a “secret garden” that could also be used as a wedding venue. The plans include a USA Pavilion with what organisers described as “Bellagio-style” fountains.Meadley told KARE 11 that organisers are planning for between 4 million and 6 million visitors during the six-month event. The organisers have said the event would bring millions of people to the southern suburbs and increase activity for local businesses.“We have a project that has moved from vision to development,” Meadley said during a presentation to the Lakeville City Council on September 21.The site is currently vacant land. It is owned by the United Christian Academy Foundation, which has agreed to sell the nearly 57-acre parcel to Expo 2031, according to the Minnesota Star Tribune.The plans for Expo 2031 go beyond the six-month exhibition. Organisers want parts of the development to remain after the event and become a longer-term site.The planned USA Pavilion is a major part of that approach. Meadley said the project needed a substantial legacy feature that would continue to exist after the Expo rather than being built only for the event. “It’s about a billion-dollar project,” Meadley told the Lakeville City Council.The current budget is just under $1 billion, according to the Minnesota Star Tribune. KARE 11 reported that the figure is more than twice the estimate given when Dakota County was pitching to host the event in 2024.Meadley said the higher figure includes the economics around the USA Pavilion, which organisers consider the project's main legacy feature. “If you look at the Eiffel Tower or the Seattle Needle (other World's Fair legacy projects) what we believed was a tower or an edifice of that type wasn’t enough,” Meadley said. “We believe there had to be something much more robust that would live on in the future.”The proposed Expo has also brought questions from people living and working near the site, particularly about its cost, traffic and whether the project will be completed.Dan Mullin, who owns an auto repair shop across a gravel road from the undeveloped land, said he had heard rumours about the Expo for months before the plans were confirmed.Mullin said he was encouraged by the renderings showing how the site could be transformed. However, he remains cautious because he has seen previous plans for the land that did not move ahead.“A couple of times a summer, it seems like there’s a whole group of people that are up there doing those (photos) where they’re all taking a scoop of dirt and throwing it and then nothing happens,” Mullin said. “I think it’s fifty-fifty that they’re gonna be able to pull it off.” He also questioned the project’s price and timeline.With millions of visitors expected over six months, managing traffic and the effect on daily life in Lakeville is another part of the planning.Meadley said organisers want visitors to arrive steadily throughout the six-month Expo rather than creating concentrated pressure on local infrastructure. Shuttle buses and other measures are being considered to help manage congestion.“We know that if people can’t move around regular and have regular everyday life during those six months of expo, we’re going to have really displeased residents of the greater metro area,” she said.Mullin said he still has questions about the project but is willing to hear more about the plans. “We don’t really know if it’s good or bad yet, I feel like it probably would be good for us,” he said.Lakeville is planning public open houses with Expo organisers so residents can ask questions about the project. The first is scheduled at City Hall on October 21 from 4pm to 7pm.
Article Summary: Minnesota has selected Lakeville as the planned host city for Expo 2031, a six- month international exhibition focused on horticulture. Organisers have signed a purchase agreement for nearly 57 acres of land near Interstate 35 and County Road 70. The Expo is scheduled to run from May to October 2031.

Article Title: In the early 1900s, a United States plant explorer tested Japanese kudzu near Washington, D.C.; later promoted for soil protection, the “wonder plant” spread across millions of acres of the South
Article Text:
A United States plant explorer tested Japanese kudzu near Washington. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

David Fairchild

planted kudzu seedlings around his home in 1902

More than 1.2 million acres were planted after the Soil Conservation Service backed kudzu

Kudzu's growth rate rises with carbon dioxide, and it spends little on woody tissue

Kudzu (

Pueraria montana

): History, Physiology, and Ecology Combine to Make a Major Ecosystem Threat

Nitrogen fixation more than doubles

nitric oxide emissions

from invaded soils

Soil erosion, brownout. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Forest Service survey data puts kudzu on about 227,000 acres of Southern forestland

Kudzu was no accident of nature: federal agencies promoted it and paid for it, and the evidence shows an ecological impact that is real but smaller than the legend suggests. The Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935 as a USDA agency and now known as the Natural Resources Conservation Service, tested, praised, and paid farmers to plant kudzu in the 1930s and 1940s, before the ecological cost was counted, as naturalist Bill Finch recounts in Smithsonian Magazine.Kudzu first reached the United States as an ornamental vine in the Japanese pavilion at the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition of 1876. A paper from the USDA Forest Service Southern Research Station picks up the story from there. David Fairchild, the plant explorer, had seen farmers in Japan using kudzu for grazing, and in 1902 he planted kudzu seedlings in his garden near Washington, D.C., to see how the plant would behave. By 1907, kudzu hay had been demonstrated in Jamestown, Virginia, a sign of growing interest in the plant as livestock feed. Fairchild, however, grew wary of it. By 1938, he had turned against the plant, and in his autobiography, The World Was My Garden, he recalled firsthand how kudzu covered bushes and climbed pines, smothering them. That account reflects Fairchild's own experience with his experiment, not an official USDA position on kudzu.C. E. Pleas, a farmer from Chipley, Florida, discovered that livestock eagerly ate kudzu. After confirming with the USDA that the plant was not poisonous, he promoted it as a forage crop through newspaper articles and pamphlets, according to Florida Memory, the Florida Department of State's archive program. He turned into an avid fan of the crop and planted 35 acres to sell as fodder. In the 1930s and 1940s, the Soil Conservation Service promoted kudzu as a means of stabilizing soil in the rapidly eroded gullies of the South, particularly in the Piedmont regions of Alabama, Georgia, and Mississippi. The agency distributed more than 85 million seedlings and paid farmers to plant the vine. The farmers were paid to plant kudzu, and more than 1.2 million acres were planted under this federal program. This number covers only the acreage planted under the federal program, not all the kudzu planted in the U.S., and Bill Finch's reporting in Smithsonian Magazine puts total plantings at a little more than a million acres by 1945.Why did the vine take so well?, published in Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences in 2004, offers part of the answer. The growth of kudzu is stimulated significantly by increased levels of CO₂, according to Irwin Forseth and Anne Innis of the University of Maryland, College Park. Because kudzu does not invest in woody structure, this growth boost could make it even more competitive as atmospheric CO₂ concentrations rise. A fast-growing plant that invests little in woody tissue can outcompete slower-growing rivals.The plant also alters the soil it grows in. Jonathan Hickman and colleagues showed this in "Kudzu (Pueraria montana) Invasion Doubles Emissions of Nitric Oxide and Increases Ozone Pollution," published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2010. The authors point to the southeastern United States as an area of particular concern: because kudzu fixes nitrogen, it drives extra nitric oxide emissions from the soil, and nitric oxide feeds ozone formation. In 2007, the team studied soils at three sites in Madison County, Georgia. In invaded soils, net nitrogen mineralization rose by up to 1,000% and net nitrification by up to 500% compared with control soils, and nitric oxide emissions were more than 100% higher (2.81 versus 1.24 ng NO‑N cm⁻² h⁻¹). Only these figures are field measurements.The researchers then fed their data into the GEOS‑Chem atmospheric chemistry model and assumed an extreme scenario in which kudzu invaded all nonagricultural, nonurban soils across nine southeastern states. Under that scenario, soil nitric oxide emissions rose by 28%, and some areas saw up to seven additional days each summer when 8-hour ozone concentrations exceeded 70 ppb. These are projections, not measurements.Kudzu is often said to cover seven million to nine million acres of the United States, but Bill Finch, writing in Smithsonian Magazine's "The True Story of Kudzu, the Vine That Never Truly Ate the South," reports that scientists reassessing its spread found nothing close to that. Forest Service survey data from 2010 shows that 227,000 acres of southern forestland contain kudzu, about one-tenth of 1 percent of the region's 200 million acres of forestland. This estimate covers forestland only, so kudzu growing on other land is not counted.The Forest Service expects the infested forestland to grow by no more than 2,500 acres a year, while some sources repeat an unsupported figure of 150,000 acres a year. The research on kudzu's ecology helps explain why the plant competes so well. Forseth and Innis (2004) attribute kudzu's edge to two physiological traits: a fast response to high CO₂ concentrations and little investment in woody tissue. Much of what people say about kudzu's ecological effects comes from testimony rather than measurement, which is why the Forest Service survey and the studies above matter. It was planted deliberately, its growth habits give it a competitive edge, and its effects on soil chemistry reach as far as the air above it. Its environmental impact is smaller than some legends suggest.
Article Summary: Kudzu first reached the United States as an ornamental vine at the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition of 1876. In the 1930s and 1940s, the Soil Conservation Service promoted kudzu as a means of stabilizing soil in the rapidly eroded gullies of the South. The agency distributed more than 85 million seedlings and paid farmers to plant the vine.

Article Title: In 1914, a Connecticut writer opened one of America’s first private songbird sanctuaries; her work helped shape a statewide bird-protection movement that still operates
Article Text:
Exterior of the Connecticut Audubon Society Birdcraft Museum & Sanctuary in Fairfield, CT. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Wright helped found the Connecticut Audubon Society in January 1898

The Friendship of Nature

Birdcraft

Field Guide to the Birds

Annie Burr Jennings

funded a 10-acre former pasture that opened as Birdcraft in 1914

Nearly 1,000 visitors in the first month drove the birds away and led to a museum

Bird-protection bills from 1907 to 1919 came out of the society Wright led

The 1957 Interstate 95 route took nearly half the land, and landmark status came in 1993

U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service staff and Audubon Connecticut. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The society now operates sanctuaries and a Hartford advocacy program

Birdcraft Sanctuary was founded in Fairfield, Connecticut, in 1914, and the Connecticut Audubon Society describes it as one of the first private songbird sanctuaries in the United States. It is a National Historic Landmark. Its creator was Mabel Osgood Wright, a writer and conservationist who had already spent years pressing for laws to protect birds. The sanctuary did not start the state's bird-protection effort so much as give it a home. Wright helped found the Connecticut Audubon Society in 1898, sixteen years earlier, and the society still operates. Its history page lists centers and sanctuaries across the state, along with an advocacy program in Hartford that has run since 1974.The Connecticut Audubon Society's history page says a small group of women in Fairfield founded it in 1898, including Wright, Helen Glover, Theodora Wheeler and Harriet Glover. A profile of Wright , written by a later chair of the society's board and republished in 2023, puts the founding in January 1898 and says Wright served as president until 1924. Wright was also a prolific author. The profile counts 27 books, beginning within 1894. Her 1895 bird guide,, was reprinted nine times and served as the most popular bird guide until Roger Tory Peterson’sappeared in 1934. She joined the founding board of the National Association of Audubon Societies in 1905, though the Connecticut society stayed independent when that group became the National Audubon Society in 1940.Wright had earlier advocated for "songbird reservations" before she made one. After she and some friends watched a play about a feather hunter who became a bird conservationist, Jennings urged that Connecticut needed a sanctuary and that Wright should create it. Jennings's gift of 10 acres in 1914, the society's history page says, let Wright create Birdcraft Sanctuary. The land was a piece of former pasture within walking distance from the train station and near the Wright residence. It contained trees and berry bushes which were favorable for the birds. Workers erected a fence designed to keep away cats, created paths, planted shrubbery, constructed a cabin for a caretaker, and dredged a pond fed by springs. Wright planned the sanctuary as both a refuge for birds and a place where people could observe them.The public reaction almost ruined the whole plan. According to the profile of Wright, nearly 1,000 visitors came in the first month, and the birds vanished. Instead of limiting access, however, the board came up with a different idea. Visitors would keep bringing dead birds and asking about them, so the caretaker, Frank Novak, who was also a taxidermist, would mount them. This resulted in the creation of a one-room museum with seasonal displays, this time funded by Jennings, the construction of which began in late November 1914 and which opened in March 1915. By July 1, 1915, the sanctuary had received 1,300 visitors, and 52 nests were recorded in its first year. It also followed the harsher management practices of its era: cats were not allowed, and predatory birds were removed as well.Her efforts transcended the fence line. According to the profile, the society she helped form backed legislation on hunting control in 1907, protection of birds and eggs from collectors in 1911, sandpipers in 1912 and the International Migratory Bird Treaty Act in 1918. It opposed a bounty on Bald Eagles in 1919. Once the bills were approved, Wright campaigned for their enforcement. Frank Chapman described Birdcraft in Bird-Lore as "an object lesson in conservation and museum methods. " Birdcraft became a model for other projects. Bird-Craft also inspired the Theodore Roosevelt Memorial Sanctuary in Oyster Bay, after Roosevelt's widow visited while seeking a fitting memorial.After Wright died in 1934, the sanctuary changed drastically. According to the Connecticut Audubon Society's profile of Wright, the construction of Interstate 95 in 1957 took nearly half of Birdcraft Sanctuary's land. The state initially offered $20,000 in compensation, and appeals failed because it did not recognize the property's value as a sanctuary. The final settlement was $42,000, which the profile says fell far short of covering the loss.However, even then, the place continued serving its purpose. Even so, the sanctuary kept serving its purpose: migrating birds still use the pond and dense vegetation between the highway and the railroad. It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1993. According to the society's Birdcraft web page, more than 150 bird species have been recorded there, and it is a federally licensed bird banding station.According to its history page, the society opened the Center at Fairfield in 1971, the Coastal Center at Milford Point in 1995 and the Center at Pomfret in 2000, and it launched its Science in Nature program in 2012. Since 1974, its Hartford advocacy program has contributed to every major environmental initiative in Connecticut. This information makes a cautious interpretation of the legacy of the sanctuary justified. Birdcraft did not found the bird protection campaign in Connecticut, as it was established by the society back in 1898. However, it provided this campaign with its public location, a way of teaching people about birds, and a record of success, and it continues to work as an organization.
Article Summary: Mabel Osgood Wright helped found the Connecticut Audubon Society in 1898. Annie Burr Jennings funded a 10-acre former pasture that opened as Birdcraft in 1914. Nearly 1,000 visitors in the first month drove the birds away and led to a museum.

Article Title: Over 50 years, a model maker built a 3,800-square-foot miniature circus by hand; it now anchors Florida’s Ringling Circus Museum
Article Text:
Miniature circus zebra balancing. Image credits Wikimedia Commons

Tibbals built wooden circus toys from 1948 and began the Howard Bros. model in 1956
