The model covers more than 3,800 square feet; counts range from 42,000 to 45,000 pieces

Tibbals collected circus materials for more than 60 years to keep the model accurate

The model premiered at the 1982 Knoxville World's Fair and moved to a center that opened in 2006

The Circus Museum dates to 1948 and added a modern-era gallery in April 2024

Tibbals Learning Center - Circus Museum - John and Mable Ringling Museum of Art. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Tibbals died on March 20, 2022, and the model remains the museum's centerpiece

In Sarasota, Florida, a miniature circus covers more than 3,800 square feet, according to The Ringling's Circus Museum teacher guide. The Ringling Circus Museum describes the Howard Bros. Circus Model as a historically accurate rendition of an early twentieth-century circus, made up of more than 42,000 pieces. It is the centerpiece of the museum's Tibbals Learning Center. One man made it. Howard Tibbals, a circus lover and philanthropist, built pieces for the model across most of his adult life, and his gifts helped pay for the building that houses it. The story covers how the model grew, how it reached Sarasota, and what else the Tibbals family left the museum.His passion predates the model itself. As Jennifer Lemmer Posey, Tibbals' curator of the circus, said in her 2024 interview with Florida State University News, he had loved circuses since childhood and was fascinated by their logistics and storytelling. According to The Ringling Circus Museum Teacher Guide, Howard Tibbals began working on his circus model at age 17, which would be about 1953. Nevertheless, the official project occurred a bit later. As Sarasota Magazine wrote in March 2022, Tibbals began working on the model in 1956, when he was 19 or 20. According to Sarasota Magazine, Tibbals spent more than 60 years building the model, which NC State Magazine says contains over 45,000 pieces.Howard Tibbals died on March 20, 2022, at the age of 85, according to Sarasota Magazine. NC State Magazine, describing Tibbals as an alumnus of the class of 1959, explained the naming of the model. Though the model is a replica of the Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus, the organization refused to use its name; hence, it was named Howard Bros. Circus.The museum's page describes the model as made up of more than 42,000 pieces in more than 3,800 square feet, while NC State Magazine reports more than 45,000 pieces. The information on the Ringling page states that visitors can witness the engineering involved in moving the entire “tented city” of the circus from town to town every day, as well as have a backstage look into the life of those who worked in the circus. Florida State University News calls the model a bird’s-eye view of a circus of the early twentieth century.Accuracy drove his collecting. Patch, reporting on a news release from The Ringling, said Tibbals gathered materials documenting circus history for more than 60 years to make sure the model was historically accurate. The digital archive collections on The Ringling's site list parts of what became the Tibbals Circus Collection, including a collection of heralds from The Ringling Circus Archives. One series, the Tibbals Circus Collection of International Newspapers, has been used to build a virtual clipping collection drawn from more than 150 newspapers dating from 1685 to 1907, most of them British. A separate set of Barnum & Bailey, Ringling Bros., and Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey programs covers 1899 to 2013, so the two collections overlap only from 1899 to 1907.The model did not begin in Sarasota. The Sarasota Herald-Tribune reported that it premiered at the 1982 World's Fair in Knoxville, Tennessee. A profile of Janice Tibbals on The Ringling's site says she and Howard married in 1991 and worked together to install the model in venues around the country. It further indicates that their donations were made in 2000 and 2008, respectively, with the state matching their donations to fund construction of the two phases of the Tibbals Learning Center. Additionally, the Tibbals Endowment was formed by their gift, providing funds for the preservation of the circus collections and staffing and programming. According to The Ringling's tribute to Tibbals, he and his wife, Janice, donated $6.5 million to fund the initial building and endow the circus program. The center opened in 2006. The Florida State University News states that Tibbals gave his name to the museum's building, catalogued his collection of circus memorabilia, and helped install the model.The model was added to the collection in the museum with a rich history behind its establishment. As seen in the above-mentioned museum page, The Ringling's first director, A. Everett "Chick" Austin, established the unique Museum of the American Circus in 1948. The museum's historic galleries feature circus wagons, a sideshow bannerline and a private turn-of-the-century Pullman railcar of John and Mable Ringling called the Wisconsin.The museum continues growing and developing. According to Florida State University News, The Greatest Show on Earth Gallery opened on April 6, 2024, with Posey as the head curator. The museum's page mentions that the gallery focuses on the period that started in 1967 when Irvin Feld bought Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey and lasted for fifty years under the supervision of the Feld family. Additionally, Florida State University News provides more information about The Ringling as the State Art Museum of Florida and a part of Florida State University, and adds that Posey collaborated closely with Tibbals while studying as a graduate student and working for more than twenty years at the museum.Once Tibbals had passed away, Sarasota Magazine reported the executive director of the museum stating that the model and the Tibbals Circus Collection were going to be his enduring legacy. As she mentioned during her speech in 2024, the passion of Tibbals was part of what she was doing. This legacy is apparent on the museum premises. A personal hobby that began with wooden toys back in 1948 and became an official project in 1956 now takes up the first floor of a building paid for by his family members in a museum that has operated a circus collection since 1948. The description provided by The Ringling itself states that it is a historically accurate depiction of an early twentieth-century circus, and it still is the highlight of any visitor's experience.
Article Summary: Howard Tibbals began working on the model in 1956, when he was 19 or 20. He collected circus materials for more than 60 years to keep the model accurate. The model premiered at the 1982 Knoxville World's Fair and moved to a center that opened in 2006. The Ringling Circus Museum describes the Howard Bros. Circus Model as a historically accurate rendition of an early twentieth-century circus.

Article Title: California thieves steal Nvidia-branded trailers expecting expensive AI hardware; find 40,000 pounds of sand instead
Article Text:
California thieves found sand inside the Nvidia-branded trailers

What was inside the stolen trailers

Why PlusAI uses sand to test autonomous trucks

How the stolen trailers were found

What police said about the theft

The connection between PlusAI and Nvidia

Two Nvidia-branded trailers belonging to autonomous-trucking company PlusAI were stolen from outside its warehouse in Fremont, California, on September 23, 2026. The trailers were associated with PlusAI's work with Nvidia on autonomous-driving technology, but instead of carrying GPUs, servers or other expensive AI equipment, each contained about 20,000 pounds of sand. The pair therefore carried roughly 40,000 pounds, or 20 tons, of sand. PlusAI uses the material as simulated cargo during autonomous-truck testing to reproduce the weight of real freight. The trailers were later discovered in nearby Newark after an acquaintance of a PlusAI executive spotted them, while police continued investigating the theft.The two trailers were parked outside PlusAI's Fremont facility when they were taken overnight. Their locks were broken and the thieves apparently arrived with tractor units, connected them to the trailers and drove away. Both trailers prominently displayed PlusAI and Nvidia branding, reflecting the companies' work in autonomous trucking and artificial intelligence.The company's autonomous-driving truck cabs remained inside the facility and were not stolen. The stolen trailers were later located in Newark, California, roughly half a mile from PlusAI's Fremont warehouse.The trailers contained about 20,000 pounds of sand each, giving them a combined load of approximately 40,000 pounds, or 20 tons. The sand was being used as simulated cargo during PlusAI's testing programme.Heavy simulated cargo allows autonomous-truck developers to reproduce the conditions of a loaded commercial vehicle without using an actual freight shipment. The added weight can be used to test how a truck responds during acceleration, braking, turning and other driving conditions.PlusAI develops autonomous-driving technology for commercial trucks, meaning its vehicles must be tested under conditions that resemble real-world freight operations. Vehicle behaviour can change significantly depending on how much weight a truck is carrying.Using sand provides a practical way to create a controlled and consistent load. Engineers can adjust the amount of weight while testing different driving scenarios, helping them study how the autonomous system and vehicle respond when operating under the demands of a loaded truck.The trailers were eventually spotted in Newark, close to PlusAI's Fremont facility. An acquaintance of a PlusAI executive reportedly noticed the trailers and sent a photograph to the executive after recognising them.The company contacted authorities, who located and recovered both trailers. The sand was still inside, allowing PlusAI to recover both the vehicles and their testing cargo.The Fremont Police Department investigated the theft after the trailers were reported missing. Security footage reportedly showed two unidentified tractor units near the PlusAI facility around the time of the incident.PlusAI said the tractor units did not belong to the company. Investigators were working to identify the people involved and determine how the trailers were taken from the facility.The Nvidia branding on the trailers reflected the companies' collaboration in autonomous trucking. PlusAI works with Nvidia on computing and artificial-intelligence technology used in autonomous vehicles.Nvidia's technology is widely used in AI development and autonomous-driving systems, making its branding highly recognisable in the technology industry. However, the trailers themselves were being used by PlusAI for autonomous-truck testing, with the confirmed cargo consisting of sand rather than Nvidia computing equipment.The theft produced an unexpected discovery when two trailers carrying prominent technology-company branding turned out to be loaded with 40,000 pounds of sand. The trailers had been taken from PlusAI's Fremont facility but were found only about half a mile away in Newark.Both trailers and their simulated cargo were recovered, while investigators continued working to identify the people responsible for the theft.
Article Summary: California thieves found sand inside the Nvidia-branded trailers. PlusAI uses the material as simulated cargo during autonomous-truck testing to reproduce the weight of real freight. The stolen trailers were later located in Newark, California, roughly half a mile from PlusAI's Fremont warehouse. The sand was still inside, allowing PlusAI to recover both the vehicles and their testing cargo.

Article Title: Over 20 years, a New York painter hand-dug a lake and planted thousands of native trees; the private landscape survives as Olana State Historic Site
Article Text:
AI representation: Hand‑dug lake at Olana State Historic Site, surrounded by thousands of native trees. Image credits: Chatgpt

A 126-acre farm bought in 1860 grew to 250 acres

Hand excavation beginning in 1860 formed the 10-acre lake over about 20 years

The Lake was overflowing in 1878 and 1879 and later fed the main house cistern

Thousands of native trees planted on land deforested by 19th-century industry

About five miles of carriage roads, including Ridge Road and Crown Hill Road in 1884

Olana, home of American landscape artist Frederic Edwin Church. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Restoration since 1966 dredged the lake and reopened views of the Hudson River

Frederic Edwin Church is best known as a Hudson River School painter, yet he treated the land around his home as a large-scale landscape composition. New York State Parks describes Olana as the 19th-century home, studio, and designed landscape of Hudson River School artist Frederic Edwin Church, his wife Isabel and their four children. The estate sits near Hudson, New York, and the state agency notes that 2026 marks the bicentennial of his birth. Two parts of that landscape are especially striking: a 10-acre lake largely excavated by hand from muck and woodlands of thousands of native trees. The Olana State Historic Site's history of the landscape explains that the lake took about twenty years to form, beginning when Church bought his first parcel of land. The lake and portions of the planted woodland survive, although both have been altered and managed over time. The Olana Partnership works with the state's parks office to care for them.In 1860, Church purchased a 126‑acre farm two months before marrying Isabel Carnes, according to the Olana Partnership’s official history of the landscape. He called the property "The Farm" and operated it as both a working and ornamental farm. Throughout the years, Church acquired additional acreage, which included the hillside known as Sienghenberg, upon which he constructed his primary residence with help from the architect Calvert Vaux.Olana's history of the landscape and its account of Church's life show that he bought 18 acres at the top of the hill in 1866 and added the 50-acre North Meadow in 1878, with further parcels bringing the estate to the 250 acres maintained today. Olana's biography of Church presents him as a farmer and landscape artist as much as a painter. It says he planted crops, kept a dairy herd, turned a swampy area into a lake and set out thousands of trees.The initial formation of the lake took place from a bog area of the property. The lake was created through hand excavation of the muck over about two decades, before machinery capable of the task existed. The process started when Church purchased his first parcel of land. Muck was not just dirt. It was fertile soil which was spread by Church on his lands as fertilizer for his planting efforts. Church also made a deal with a laborer, who cleared muck in return for half of it. The construction of the dam ensured that the basin would be filled with water, and the lake's shape followed the contours of the land. The lake's outline and still surface echo Inbocht Bay, several miles south on the Hudson River.According to Olana's history of the landscape, activity surged in 1878 and 1879, when Church wrote that the lake was overflowing and his birch canoe was ready. The basin was already holding water and in use while the twenty years of excavation were still underway. The lake served purposes other than aesthetic ones. It was used for boating, skating, and fishing. The lake also supplied water. Church installed a system that pumped it up to a cistern in the main house, and water is still pumped from the lake to a water tower near the main house today.The woods solved a particular problem. The history of Olana notes that the Hudson River functioned as an industrial river that led to New York City throughout the nineteenth century, and much of the land near the river, which included the Olana property, had been denuded as a result of industry and commercial activity. Church planted thousands of trees in the region, including maple, birch, hickory, hemlock, chestnut, pine, and oak. Church noted that for several years after he selected the site, his thoughts did not veer far from it. The plantings served varied purposes. Some were used to create dense woods, others to frame distant views and still others to conceal structures like the stables. He arranged the trees in the meadow as well as in groups and singly, and lined the roads with them.Church linked the lake and woodlands through the roads. One can take a self-guided walk through the farm, the orchards and the lake formed out of swampland, says New York State Parks. The road system of the estate extends for about five miles. Lake Road cut through the woods adjacent to the lake and afforded views of the lake from the park and house above it.There were two roads built in 1884, namely Ridge Road and Crown Hill Road, which guided people through a unique land formation. In an August 1887 letter to the writer Charles Dudley Warner, cited in the journal Art History, Church said he was busy "landscape architecturing." In an 1884 letter, according to Olana's history of the landscape, he wrote that building roads let him make more and better landscapes than "tampering with canvas and paint" in the studio. Dynamite was used to blast certain routes, and workers covered the roads with red shale mined from the property.Olana was preserved from demolition in 1966, and from that time restoration and stewardship have tried to reclaim elements of the design created by Church while preserving Olana as a historic public site. The work has included dredging the lake and managing aquatic invasive plants so that the full water surface stays visible. In addition, second growth of woodland and invasive plants have been removed to restore the view of the Hudson River, and the fields of farms have been uncovered together with stone walls. The North Meadow restoration is under way. The place that visitors walk around is thus not only a historic document but also a living project. A lake dug largely by hand and thousands of trees planted under one artist's direction, created a personal landscape that later became a public one.
Article Summary: Olana is the home, studio, and designed landscape of Hudson River School artist Frederic Edwin Church, his wife Isabel and their four children. The estate sits near Hudson, New York, and the state agency notes that 2026 marks the bicentennial of his birth. The lake was created through hand excavation of the muck over about two decades, before machinery capable of the task existed.

Article Title: In 1977, a Canadian student lost his class ring in the Barbados surf; 47 years later, a metal detectorist recovered it from the ocean and traced him down
Article Text:
Representative image of a ring on the left and the Barbados surf beach on the right. (Image Credits: Leonardo.ai).

A post-hurricane recovery lead to the discovery

Representative image of a metal detectorist along shoreline. (Image Credit: Pexels)

An unexpected package on a birthday

After nearly half a century at the bottom of the ocean, a Canadian university graduate’s lost gold class ring has been returned to him. Frederick Morgan Perigo lost the class ring back in 1977 and now it has been successfully retrieved. The reunion was made possible by Alex Davis, an enthusiast for lost items who found the ring while scanning the seabed with a metal detector. The discovery eventually set off an international tracking effort to return the heirloom back to its original owner.The separation occurred during a family excursion to the ocean with his wife, and their two young sons. While wading into the water, a sudden powerful wave knocked his youngest son off balance. As Perigo jumped to the boy's rescue, the ring inadvertently slipped from his hand. Perigo said in an official statement that he never had time to react before the ring was gone. He and his family searched the water for it in the moments after, according to CBS News, but had no luck and assumed at the time it was lost for good.The storm that may have possibly exposed the ring wasn't a minor squall. According to the National Hurricane Center's report , Hurricane Beryl was the earliest record of a Category 5 hurricane in the Atlantic basin.Subsequently, Barbados was put under a hurricane warning as the storm passed through the Windward Islands in July 2024. Davis has theorized that this violent storm activity had washed away the coastal sediments, ultimately laying bare years of submerged items under the sand including the graduate's long-lost memento.“So areas where it was like a beautiful sandy beach, suddenly you can see all these rocks exposed,” Davis explained. “With that sort of in mind, I was like right, are there some areas now I want to go to where they seem like a lot of sand has been pulled out?”While scanning through an area littered with vintage coins dating back to the 1970s and 1980s, Davis’s underwater detector triggered an alert, prompting him to dig through dead coral and rocks before he saw the flash of gold. Despite having been vulnerable to shifting sands and seawater for 47 years, the ring’s structural framework remained intact. Upon inspecting his find, the diver noticed three identifying markers: Perigo’s school name, the graduation year of 1965, and his initials, “FMP”.In order to locate the owner of the ring, Davis wrote a digital message along with pictures of the jewelry to the administrative staff at McMaster University in Hamilton. The task was complicated by the fact that in the university's alumni database Perigo was registered under his middle name, Morgan, instead of "F," which his initials on the ring suggested. Upon receiving the inquiry Laura Escalante, an alumni officer, started an extensive search of enrolled students from the institution's records dating back to the mid-1960s. Escalante successfully cross-referenced the clues from the ring until finally landing on Frederick Morgan Perigo, a mathematics major.Once a direct contact was established by the University, following Perigo’s verification on exact circumstances of his loss, Escalante connected him to Davis. Davis organised an international FedEx delivery from Barbados to have the long-lost keepsake returned to its owner. The package arrived in the hands of Perigo on the day before his birthday, completing a full circle of forty-seven-years. The unexpected timing of the arrival turned the retrieved memento into a celebratory birthday present for the Canadian resident, who was deeply moved by the collaborative efforts of his alma mater and the recovery diver.
Article Summary: A Canadian university graduate's lost gold class ring has been returned to him. Frederick Morgan Perigo lost the class ring back in 1977 and now it has been successfully retrieved. The reunion was made possible by an enthusiast for lost items who found the ring while scanning the seabed with a metal detector.

Article Title: Child, forced marriages of minority girls in Pakistan flagged at UN event
Article Text:
UN rights event highlights risks faced by girls in Pakistan’s child marriages (ANI photo)

The impact of child and forced marriages on girls in Pakistan, particularly those from minority communities, was discussed at a side event during the 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva.Speakers at the event raised concerns about girls being married at a young age and the consequences for their education, health and basic rights. The event was reported by Global Human Rights Defence, a UN ECOSOC-accredited human rights organisation.Naveed Walter, president of Human Rights Focus Pakistan and a human rights defender, pointed to the scale of child rights violations in Pakistan and the vulnerability of children who enter marriage at an early age.“Most recently, UNICEF gave the data about Pakistan. Ninety million women and children and girls have been affected by child rights violations. And of them, 4.8 million were under 15 years of age,” Walter said.Walter said early marriage can leave girls without access to basic education and expose them to serious health risks, particularly during pregnancy.“You know, dear excellencies and dear audience, that during pregnancy, millions of children have died.And you know, under 30 per cent of the children who get married even have basic education,” he said.The discussion also focused on Sindh, where women's rights activist Shagufta Kandhro highlighted the situation of girls who are married before reaching adulthood.“According to the National Commission on the Rights of the Child, 84,000 children between the ages of 10 and 17 are married, widowed and separated. Many of them have already left school, and many face serious health risks,” Kandhro said.Kandhro said 21% of young women in Sindh had been married before turning 18. She also flagged concerns around teenage pregnancies and limited access to maternal healthcare.According to her, Pakistan sees an estimated 61,000 pregnancies among girls aged 15 to 19 each year. Only 44% of pregnant girls in this age group receive at least four antenatal visits, she said.Kandhro also cited anaemia among girls in Sindh, putting the figure at 61.9%. She described this as the highest rate among the provinces.The speakers urged stronger safeguards for women and children and called for greater international attention to child and forced marriage, which they linked to gender-based violence.
Article Summary: UN rights event highlights risks faced by girls in Pakistan’s child marriages. Women's rights activist Shagufta Kandhro highlighted the situation of girls who are married before reaching adulthood. She also flagged concerns around teenage pregnancies and limited access to maternal healthcare.

Article Title: Motorcycle-borne gunmen kill 3 cops in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
TTP suspicion after 3 traffic cops killed in Pakistan gun attack (ANI file photo)

Three traffic police officers were killed and three others injured in a gun attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Monday, the Associated Press cited police.The attack took place in Wazirabad Bazaar in Tank district when suspected militants on motorcycles opened fire on a vehicle carrying the traffic police.The attackers fled the area after the shooting, local police official Jamshed Khan said.No group has claimed responsibility for the latest attack. Police are likely to suspect the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has carried out several attacks in the region. The TTP is a separate group from Afghanistan’s Taliban but is allied with it.The attack on police officials came two days after 'fidayeen' bomb blast in Dera Ismail Khan city in the same province. The suicide bombing killed at least 13 people and wounded over 30 others.Gunmen also opened fire on an ambulance that arrived at the scene. The TTP claimed responsibility for that attack.Pakistan has repeatedly accused Afghanistan’s Taliban government of allowing TTP militants to operate from Afghan territory and carry out attacks in Pakistan.Kabul has denied the allegations and said it does not allow its territory to be used against other countries.
Article Summary: Three traffic police officers were killed and three others injured in a gun attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Monday. Police are likely to suspect the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has carried out several attacks in the region. The TTP is a separate group from Afghanistan’s Taliban but is allied with it.

Article Title: 20-year-old Azerbaijani woman allegedly drugged, gang-raped in Pakistan's Lahore
Article Text:
Azerbaijani woman, 20, allegedly drugged and gang-raped in Lahore; 3 booked (AP file photo)

A 20-year-old woman from Azerbaijan was allegedly gang-raped by three men in Lahore after being taken to a flat in the Defence Housing Authority area, news agency PTI cited police on Sunday.The incident allegedly took place after the woman, who came to Pakistan from Baku for business, was taken to a cafe by two women late on September 25. Police said three men joined them at the cafe around 11 pm and later offered to drop them in their vehicle.Instead, the men allegedly took the Azerbaijani woman to a flat, where they gave her an intoxicating substance and sexually assaulted her, according to police.She was later left near Lahore's Ghazi Interchange. The suspects allegedly took her iPhone before abandoning her.Police officer Anjum Bashir said the woman had been staying in Lahore's Raiwind area since arriving in Pakistan more than two weeks ago.Police have registered a case against three men and identified the main accused. Raids are being conducted to arrest the suspects, while their names have also been placed on the stop list to prevent them from leaving the country.The vehicle allegedly used in the incident has been recovered from the house of a relative of the main accused, Bashir said.Investigators are also examining the role of the two women who allegedly took the victim to the cafe.The woman has undergone a medical examination and police have registered the case under relevant provisions of the Pakistan Penal Code.
Article Summary: Azerbaijani woman, 20, allegedly drugged and gang-raped in Lahore; 3 booked. Incident allegedly took place after the woman was taken to a cafe by two women. Police said three men joined them at the cafe and later offered to drop them in their vehicle.

Article Title: 'Don't go back like this': Pakistan minister's throat-cut gesture to Afghan journalist backfires - video
Article Text:
Pak minister’s throat-cut gesture to Afghan journalist

Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif has faced criticism on social media over a threat-like gesture he made towards an Afghan woman journalist who questioned him about Pakistan's ties with the Taliban and its response to the treatment of Afghan women.The incident took place on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.The video clearly shows that journalist asked Asif what message Pakistan had for the Taliban over their policies toward Afghan women and why Islamabad had not challenged those policies when the Taliban were considered friends."What's your message to the Taliban now? To change their policy towards Afghan women? Why at the beginning, Pakistan didn't teach them that," the journalist asked, according to a video of the exchange shared on social media.Asif interrupted her without answering the question and pointed towards her attire."Don't go back like this over there. They will... otherwise they will..," he said, while making a hand gesture across his neck.The gesture drew strong condemnation online, with several social media users saying it appeared to imply that the journalist could be killed if she returned to Afghanistan. Users also criticised Asif and the men accompanying him for laughing after his remarks.A user on X wrote: "This is an utterly disgraceful way for a senior government minister to respond to a woman asking a serious question.""A woman asking about the suffering of Afghan women deserved an answer not intimidation, mockery, and laughter," he added.The journalist's question centred on the Taliban's policies towards Afghan women and Pakistan's position on them. Social media users said the response and the gesture were inappropriate and appeared to carry a threat of violence.The incident comes amid fresh tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan, with Islamabad carrying out aerial and drone strikes inside Afghanistan early Thursday.The Taliban also confirmed to news agency Reuters that 28 "fighters" were killed after crossing from Pakistan into eastern Afghanistan. The ruling-authority in Kabul also added that most of them were former Afghan security personnel.Pakistan called the strikes as "precision attacks" on 10 locations. Federal information minister Atauallah Tarar said the operation was carried out in response to drones launched from Afghanistan a day earlier.According to Dawn, Tarar said in a post on X that the strikes targeted locations allegedly used for launching and storing drones. He described the operation as "deliberate, precise, calibrated and proportionate and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan".Afghanistan has warned Pakistan of "dire consequences" over the strikes, describing them as blatant aggression."In this criminal aggression, four of our fellow Afghan compatriots have been martyred. The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan strongly condemns these blind and cowardly attacks in the harshest terms, considering them a flagrant violation of all principles, a blatant aggression, and a crime," Afghan government spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid said.Cross-border hostilities between the two neighbours have continued in recent weeks, with Pakistan carrying out military action, including aerial strikes, inside Afghanistan.
Article Summary: Pak defence minister Khawaja Asif made a threat-like gesture to an Afghan journalist. The journalist asked him about Pakistan's ties with the Taliban and its response to the treatment of Afghan women. Social media users said the response and the gesture were inappropriate and appeared to carry a threat of violence.

Article Title: At least 13 dead in suicide bomb blast near police post in northwestern Pakistan
Article Text:
Also Read:

Pakistani Taliban claims responsibility

Poll Vote & Share your view What is the most important action the government should take in response to the recent attack? Increase security at checkpoints Strengthen military operations Enhance community awareness programs Focus on diplomacy with militant groups 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

(With AP inputs)

At least 13 people were killed and around 35 others wounded on Saturday when a suicide bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at a roadside police checkpoint in northwestern Pakistan, police and rescue officials said.The attack took place in Dera Ismail Khan, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Local police chief Safdar Baloch said most of the injured were security personnel and passersby, with some in critical condition.According to Baloch, gunmen later opened fire on an ambulance carrying victims to a nearby hospital, killing a rescue worker and injuring two others.Two women and a child were also among those killed in the suicide bombing, he added.The Pakistan i Taliban, or Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack. The TTP is separate from, but allied with, the Afghan Taliban, which returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021 after the US withdrew its troops.Pakistan has witnessed a surge in militant attacks in recent years, many of them claimed by the TTP and the outlawed Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), a separatist group primarily active in neighbouring Balochistan province.Islamabad has repeatedly accused the Afghan Taliban of allowing TTP members to operate from Afghan soil and have demanded that Kabul prevent cross-border attacks into Pakistan. Afghan authorities have denied allowing their territory to be used for attacks against other countries.Dera Ismail Khan is near South Waziristan, a former militant stronghold where the Pakistani military has carried out several operations in recent years.In December 2023, a suicide bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at the main gate of a police station in Dera Ismail Khan, killing at least 23 security personnel in one of the deadliest attacks in the area. It was claimed by Tehreek-e-Jihad Pakistan, a small militant group believed to be an offshoot of the TTP.
Article Summary: The attack took place in Dera Ismail Khan, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. The Pakistan i Taliban, or Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility. The TTP is separate from, but allied with, the Afghan Taliban.

Article Title: Pakistan govt puts Islamabad on lockdown as Imran Khan’s party pushes ahead with march
Article Text:
Islamabad locked down as PTI prepares for Imran Khan march

Leaders of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party have vowed to press ahead with nationwide demonstrations demanding his release, as authorities tightened security in Islamabad ahead of the planned march.More than 1,000 shipping containers, many reinforced with spikes, have been placed to block roads, while sandbags have been positioned on bridges and a key highway leading into the capital has been closed. Public gatherings have also been banned in Islamabad, with 22,000 police and other security personnel deployed across the city.The government has also deployed security personnel in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and closed the main highway linking the provincial capital, Peshawar, with Islamabad. The sweeping security measures have fuelled anger and frustration in the capital, with several businesses struggling to receive supplies.The measures to prevent Khan’s PTI from proceeding with the march come amid mounting concerns over the treatment of the former prime minister, who has been in jail since August 2023 following convictions in multiple cases.On Friday, PTI leaders announced that they would postpone the start of the march to October 4, a week after the original September 27 date, saying they hoped the delay would put further pressure on the government.The planned protest also comes amid the detention of three of Imran Khan’s sisters. Aleema Khan was detained last week, followed by Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, who were ordered to remain in custody for 30 days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance.
Article Summary: More than 1,000 shipping containers, many reinforced with spikes, have been placed to block roads. Sandbags have been positioned on bridges and a key highway leading into the capital has been closed. Public gatherings have also been banned in Islamabad, with 22,000 police and other security personnel deployed.

Article Title: Pakistan goes bananas over giant gorillas dancing to Bollywood songs
Article Text:
Clips of these larger-than-life performers have been spreading rapidly online (Photo: AFP)

Pakistanis are going bananas over a trend that has crossed the Indian border: Giant gorillas, dancing to Bollywood music.Clips of these larger-than-life performers have been spreading rapidly online, turning them into the surprise stars of weddings, birthdays and other festivities.In the videos, guests can be seen joining in alongside the costumed entertainers, many of them visibly delighted by the unusual addition to their celebrations. The performers swing their oversized arms to pounding DJ tracks while partygoers gather round and dance, creating a lively, comic spectacle that has quickly drawn attention across social media.Behind the trend in Lahore is Shayen Zahoor, who runs Gorilla.co.pk, a business offering giant dancing gorilla acts for events across the city.Speaking to AFP, Zahoor explained how quickly the idea took off. He said the costume was ordered in early April and arrived by the end of the same month, after which the team wasted no time putting it to use.Once the suit arrived, he and his team lost no time getting started."We uploaded a reel on Instagram, and within just two days it reached a million views," Zahoor recalled.The overwhelming response convinced them to treat the venture as a serious business, and bookings soon began pouring in, with the public reaction proving remarkably enthusiastic."On the very first day, we received approximately 1,200 to 1,300 messages," he said, describing how curious would-be customers flooded his inbox.Many wanted to know whether the costume had genuinely arrived, what it would cost to book, and other practical details before making up their minds.What began as a single Instagram reel has since snowballed into a full-fledged entertainment phenomenon, with giant gorillas now a familiar, if unlikely, fixture at Pakistani celebrations.
Article Summary: Giant dancing gorillas have become a popular feature at Pakistani celebrations. The performers swing their oversized arms to pounding DJ tracks while partygoers gather round. A single Instagram reel has since snowballed into a full-fledged entertainment phenomenon. The trend has even crossed the Indian border.

Article Title: Pakistan govt crackdown forces PTI retreat? Imran's party likely to postpone Sept 27 Islamabad march
Article Text:
Imran Khan has been in jail since 2023

Pakistan minister says PTI has 'run away'

(With PTI inputs)

The Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) has decided to postpone its planned march to Islamabad from September 27 to October 4, party insiders said on Friday.The PTI had planned the march to the capital to demand the release of its incarcerated founder and former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan . The decision to delay the protest apparently came in response to the tough measures taken by the federal government to prevent it.According to PTI sources, the decision was taken at a party meeting and will be formally announced by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister and PTI leader Sohail Afridi.Earlier in the day, Afridi had asserted at a press conference in Peshawar that the planned long march would go ahead despite road blockades and other measures. However, he expressed concern over reports of nails being driven into roads at the provincial boundaries, questioning whether a conspiracy to “cut” Khyber Pakhtunkhwa off from the rest of Pakistan had formally begun.“Our long march will definitely take place. This time, we will definitely come out. Put nails on the roads, place containers or fire bullets, we will come out. We will end this corrupt system of fake rulers,” he told reporters.“Pakistan will not break at any cost and we will save Pakistan,” he added.Cricketer-turned-politician Khan, 73, has been held at Rawalpindi’s high-security Adiala Jail since 2023, when he was arrested following his conviction in a corruption case.Pakistan information minister Ataullah Tarar reacted to the reports by saying the PTI had “run away” because it had made “no preparations” for the march to Islamabad.“There are no preparations for the PTI’s long march either, and that is why they have backed out of this protest. If they have the courage, let them come and hold the march,” Tarar said.The federal government had placed shipping containers along Islamabad’s main roads, allowing them to be closed at short notice ahead of the planned march.Hotels in the Faizabad area of Rawalpindi had been closed, while restaurants and shopkeepers were directed to shut their businesses. Guest houses and transport terminals in Faizabad had also been ordered to close from Friday night.Thousands of security personnel were deployed in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, the capital’s twin city and home to Pakistan Army headquarters, to control Khan’s supporters.Tensions over the planned protest continued despite PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan urging the government to open negotiations and warning against confronting political workers with force.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) has decided to postpone its planned march to Islamabad from September 27 to October 4. The PTI had planned the march to the capital to demand the release of its founder and former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan. Khan has been held at Rawalpindi’s high-security Adiala Jail since 2023, when he was arrested following his conviction in a corruption case.

Article Title: 'Could endanger his life': Imran Khan's son warns against Adiala jail protest
Article Text:
Imran Khan's son warns against Adiala jail protest

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan 's son Kasim Khan has urged Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters not to march towards Rawalpindi's Adiala jail during the party's planned September 27 protest, warning that such a move could be used by Pakistani authorities as a pretext for a "counter" assault on the prison and put his father's life at risk.The warning comes ahead of the PTI's planned protest and march, which is being held to demand Imran Khan's release.The former premier has been in prison since August 2023 following convictions in multiple cases.In a post on X, Kasim said he had been asked to appeal to supporters against gathering near Adiala jail."I’ve been instructed to call on the public not to attempt to march or protest nearby Adiala jail on 27. I’ve heard from sources that this may be used as an excuse for the establishment to launch a “counter” assault on the jail (Which my father is being held in), which could endanger his life. Please do not give them any reasons for “accidents” to happen to my father during the protest," Kasim's post read.His appeal comes as security measures have been stepped up across Punjab ahead of the PTI mobilisation.The Punjab government has imposed Section 144 across the province from September 23 to October 5, restricting public gatherings of five or more people on roads and in public places. Authorities have also sought the deployment of Pakistan Rangers in Rawalpindi, Attock, Jhelum and Mianwali.The restrictions have been imposed citing security concerns. A provincial notification referred to a "serious and imminent threat" to public peace and safety from militant and terrorist organisations and hostile intelligence agencies.The planned protest comes amid the detention of three of Imran Khan's sisters. Aleema Khan was detained last week, followed by Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, who were detained for 30 days under the Punjab maintenance of public order ordinance.On Thursday, the Lahore high court refused to immediately suspend the detention orders against Uzma and Noreen. The court issued notices to the respondents and sought their replies before taking up the plea further.The detentions have added to tensions ahead of the September 27 mobilisation.According to Dawn, lawyers for Uzma and Noreen told the Lahore high court that the two women were "non-political" and had been detained without sufficient legal justification. The court decided to wait for the authorities' response before ruling on their request to suspend the detention orders.Kasim had earlier criticised the detention of his aunts and other relatives and called for international attention to the issue.“This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr. Uzma and Noreen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez, have now been abducted as well. They have broken into my aunties' and cousins' houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. No reasons for arrest have been stated," he said in a post on X.Pakistani authorities have said the preventive detentions and restrictions are linked to public-order and security concerns. The Punjab government's notification specifically cited threats from militant organisations and other security risks while announcing the province-wide restrictions.The September 27 PTI protest is expected to add to the political and security pressure surrounding Imran Khan's continued incarceration, with authorities tightening restrictions and increasing security in areas linked to the planned mobilisation.
Article Summary: Kasim Khan urges supporters not to march towards Rawalpindi's Adiala jail during the party's planned September 27 protest. He warns that such a move could be used as a pretext for a "counter" assault on the prison and put his father's life at risk. Security measures have been stepped up across Punjab ahead of the protest.

Article Title: Watch: Pakistan PM runs away from questions on Hafeez Saeed at UN
Article Text:
Pak PM skips questions at UN

Hafiz Saeed named in terror cases

India hits out at Pakistan at UN

Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday declined to answer questions from reporters about Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) founder Hafiz Saeed during his visit to the United Nations headquarters for the 81st UN General Assembly.As Sharif entered the UN headquarters, reporters asked him, “Prime Minister, when will you stop harbouring terrorists?” Sharif did not respond. Later, as he left the premises, he was again asked when Pakistan would prosecute Saeed, but the prime minister once again declined to answer.Hafiz Muhammad Saeed, founder of the proscribed LeT, is a designated terrorist under India's Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act and is wanted as an accused in the 26/11 Mumbai terror attack case.The National Investigation Agency has also named Saeed as an accused in its supplementary chargesheet in the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack case. The NIA has alleged that Pakistan-based LeT operatives were involved in the attack and has named Saeed as Accused No. 8 in the alleged larger conspiracy.A day earlier, India criticised Pakistan at the United Nations, accusing Islamabad of focusing on territorial claims and cross-border terrorism instead of addressing its economic and domestic challenges.Exercising India's right of reply at the UN Human Rights Council, Indian diplomat Kshitij Tyagi said Pakistan should focus on development rather than “coveting territory of others or exporting terror”.Tyagi also accused Pakistan of suppressing civilians in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and referred to reports of deaths, arrests and restrictions on essential supplies including food, fuel and medicine.
